text: England won the football last night, but there are women out there that won't be celebrating. Domestic violence increases by 26% when a national team plays football, by 38% if they lose, 11% the day after, regardless of the outcome. And alcohol-related abuse can rise by almost 50% with an England victory. Domestic abuse can affect anyone, but women are disproportionately affected, and women are far more likely to experience severe, continued and life-threatening abuse. Now, let's be clear. Football does not cause domestic abuse. Abusers cause domestic abuse. But major football tournaments can act as a trigger. The lady in the video talks about the connection between national team games, in this case England, and domestic abuse. She makes several claims, but in this video I want to concentrate on the one that says that domestic violence increases by 26% when a national team plays football, by 38% if they lose, and by 11% the day after. The numbers trace back to one paper. Can the FIFA World Cup football tournament be associated with an increase in domestic abuse? It was first published online in 2013 and later appeared in the 2014 issue of the Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency. Real study, but as always, the details matter. The study didn't look at every national team, every football match, or all domestic abuse everywhere. It looked at police-recorded domestic abuse incidents from one police force in northwest England, Lancashire, during three World Cups, 2002, 2006, and 2010. And the authors themselves state that it is a relatively small study. But here's what they found. On days when England played, there were around 79 reported domestic abuse incidents on average. On days when England didn't play, there were about 58. Then, after controlling for things like day of the week and year, the model found a 26% increase when England won or drew, a 38% increase when England lost, and an 11% increase the day after an England match. So the short answer is, yes, the quoted numbers are mostly accurate. Now, does this mean football causes domestic abuse? No. And the lady in the video mentions that too. Researchers are also careful about that. Most probably, football is not a magic spell where someone watches a penalty shootout and suddenly forgets how to behave like a human being. The study suggests that football may stack several risk factors on the same day. Major tournaments happen in summer. People may drink more alcohol. Emotions are higher. Fans identify strongly with the national team. People gather at home or in pubs. There is excitement, tension, disappointment, rivalry, and sometimes aggression. And if someone is already abusive, that environment can make things worse, especially after a loss. So, to wrap it up, the information she presented is generally true and backed by a study. Also, later in the video, she makes a point I actually agree with. She's not saying people shouldn't celebrate football. She's saying, celebrate, but also remember that around these big games, the risk of domestic abuse can increase for some people behind closed doors. And honestly, that is a fair message.
